sentences.text: You know, I take a high speed ferry into the city.
We're in a lovely little community.
This meeting is being recorded.
And which is great because it reminds me of my hometown, which is Vancouver.
But so I kind of live a Vancouver lifestyle, you know, taking boats into the office kind of thing.
And it sounds pretty idyllic, but most of my companions on the boat are all Wall street traders.
And so even sometimes it get a little sharpish sharper than Vancouver, that's for sure.
I see God.
Yeah.
So not all great.
All right.
I don't know which.
Which side of the boat I'd be sitting because I'm kind of bit of both.
All I'd say is that around bonus time, I feel like less of a person.
There's two.
There's two types of people in Manhattan.
Those in the finance industry and those that wish they were.
Okay.
Yeah, well, that's interesting.
Okay, well, let's get you over to the finance industry as quick as possible.
We just need to get you a nice big exit.
That'll be, that'll be your bonus check.
Yeah.
You know, ironically, we are planning a process later in the year.
You know, the, the plan is sort of like a September kind of time frame of 2026.

But, but you know, it's funny, you're the third conversation that's kind of come walking in the door and, and some folks are happy to kind of wait for the process and other folks are, are a little bit eager to kind of get an early conversation or early look, as it were.
Yeah, well, our specialty really is off market stuff, so we would be looking to get in there before you got the process up and running.
But we do work on the sell side as well.
So when it comes to September next year, if you, if you are still ready to go to market, then I'd be happy to speak to you then as well.
Yeah, I have to admit, I think we're going forward with Oberon Securities.
Seema Vasa, she's the one that did that recent prime deal.
Seem as a good friend, known her for years and years.
And John Sepala is her partner at Oberon.
But the two of them, you know, we've gone through the valuation discussions and you know, looked at the year on year growth rates and, and are charting a path for September.
To be, to be completely blunt, the tariffs messed with our world last year.
So the reason why we're thinking September is we want to get clear of the negative impact that the, you know, what happened with the tariffs was a lot of our clients freaked out, right.
Like anybody in the shoe industry.
So Vans and Crocs were both victims of the, of the tariffs.
Anybody in the retail industry, you know, Macy's victim of the tariffs.
So, so definitely, you know, in our world it's like, hey, that was a, that was a one time aberration.
Let's not bake that into the exit.
Let's get past that one time aberration.
And, and, and then, you know, shop ourselves.
So, so that's the, that's the thinking behind it, you know, and, and, and Vans is looking to come back on board.

One of the problems was, is that these, the CFOs at these companies like freaked out and overreacted, you know, and, and I have to admit it was the right thing to do from their perspective because it's still not resolved and the Supreme Court is deciding whether it was even legal in the first place.
But what's kind of happened is Q2 and Q3 were a bit of a dead zone for people in the, you know, footwear fashion.
You know, we don't make clothing or shoes outside of China anymore.
And retail, basically they've gotten a lot of funds returned to them in Q4 of this year because the CFO is like, all right, our tariff exposure action wasn't as bad as we anticipated.
And so, you know, here's some of your money back.
So for us, this year is A tale of Q1 was absolutely record breaking.
Q2 and Q3 were underwhelming and then Q4 is now springing back really hard.
Okay, so you had a strange year by the sounds of it.
Yeah, it was not a normal year.
So your expertise is in the sort of tween and Gen Z market.
Yeah, we've been at this a while.
Y Pulse has existed since 2004, but it's really kind of had three lives, as it were.
And the current life that it's on is this.
Syndicated Insights.

So we spend three and a half million dollars collecting over 400,000 interviews across seven countries, packaging up those results, you know, databasing all the answers and, and, and basically selling that to as many clients as we can.
And we have over 100 clients.
And our, our clients are companies like Apple and Amazon and Netflix and Google and YouTube.
They're like really big companies largely because you've got to be a big company to have a differentiated marketing strategy that targets youth.
Right.
Small and medium sized companies, their customers, everybody.
And they're, you know, they're just trying to market to everybody simultaneously.
But the really big brands know that, okay, you know, there's niche audiences and there's niche platforms to access those audiences.
So I have to have a dedicated youth marketing strategy as opposed to a generic marketing strategy.
So all of our customers are like Fortune 500 companies.
They're just really, really big customers and they stick with us a long time.
There's not a lot of alternatives.
There used to be, but over time they've sort of dissipated and we've eaten some of the competitors that we've had over time.
So, you know, I would say that it's nowadays it's us or Insights family out of Manchester.
Are you familiar with them at all?
Insights family?
No.
Is that Manchester in the uk?
Yep, Manchester, uk.
And definitely I would say that, you know, if you've got a UK client that's looking to, to conquer the world, you know, they're, they're in 22 countries, we're in seven countries.

We go a lot deeper than they do, you know, and of course, because they're in 20, we're about the same revenues, you know, they're spread across 22 countries and they might ask 200 questions annually and we're in seven countries and we ask a thousand questions annually.
So we've got sort of five times the depth but, you know, one third the coverage.
Yeah, that's interesting.
Taking a slightly different approach.
Our client's actually based in New York as well, so it'll be a. Yeah, most of our clients are US based.
So do you actually execute on any of this stuff or is there any like sort of bespoke strategy or is it all built into your sort of platform products?
So, so we do have about 15% of our revenues are this sort of bespoke.

So when Apple asks, you know, to better understand college students laptop purchase decisions, we're not going to, we're not going to shoo them away, but we do, we do have the services side of things limited to our subscribers.

So if you were a random coming off the street and said, I want to do a youth Insights project, we'd say, sorry, we're Busy with our 100 subscribers and helping them out on their last mile decisions and product innovations.
But here's what a subscription package looks like.
And then one of the reasons, Andrew, I'll be completely upfront, you know, we've never had successful conversations with other services companies.
So we're not really an agency, we're more of a platform.
Yeah.
And like a SaaS business model, right?
Yeah.
Subscribing and recurring annual subscriptions.
Right, Exactly.
And those tend to get valued at like a 4 to 8 multiple on revenues, whereas services is kind of like a one to two.
So, so if, if your client is a services company and they want to get into the youth space, they should buy a youth services company, not a youth platform.
Because it'd be, you know, it wouldn't be accretive, it'd be dilutive for them.
Right.
You know, they get valued at one to two times, we get valued at four to eight times.
How, how are you going to reconcile those two valuations?
And we wouldn't be enough revenue to sort of drive their valuations up.
I'll give you a great example.
Gartner.
Gartner, you know the, the IT information services provider.
Gartner once got a new CEO and he's like, wow, you know, we could make so much money on services.
Let's, let's do that.
He leaned into services and Wall street rewarded him by cutting his share price in half.
Because that recurring predictable subscription based model is worth a lot more than the.
Gosh, we start every year with zero in terms of forward revenues and we sort of figure it out on the fly on a project by project basis.
Yeah, well, the market's a little bit more complex than that now nowadays, I would say, Dan, but yeah, I think you've, you've got it right.

Obviously you know what you're talking about and you've had the valuation done, but a lot of marketing services companies, they do now have insights and they do have a lot of SaaS business models as well.
If they don't have them, they have to buy into them because just for the exact reasons you've given.
But also it makes them a lot more stable for long term investment and exits if they're looking for it first is the services themselves.
Yeah, I mean it's low multiples and also a bit of a roller coaster.
It sounds like you guys have had a bit of fun over the last couple of quarters.

But services businesses can be even worse because like you say, they don't have subscribers that they can fall back on, so they just get killed within a few months, which is a huge risk obviously for investors.
Hence the pricing is so much different.
So you guys are looking to get out or start the conversation to get out at the end of the day next year.
What's, what's been happening with the people that have knocked on the door so far?
Are you just sort of entertaining initial conversation?
Almost feels like it's not really worth it until you get to September next year, I guess.
Yeah, you know, the, the target for us, for the board is sort of a 20 million exit which is you know, kind of high three, low four based on revenue multiples.
And so it's sort of a matter of, you know, that's kind of the, the price point that we want to exit at.
And, and you know, listen, I don't think we're there right now.
Right.
If you look at our trailing 12 months and the, you know, the revenue people would, would say, you know, you're not worth 20 million.
And I probably agree with them.
Right.
We're not today.
But, but after, after building this thing for 17 years, you know, I probably want to go out at a time when, when we're not at our worst possible look.
Based on a couple of headquarters, do.
You mind me asking what your training 12 months was?
Sure, yeah.
In terms of revenues, be like 5.85 with 85% of that subscriptions and 15% of that services.

And I'm told that as long as I keep services under 15%, even know it doesn't get repriced, the second starts to get to 20% or higher, then you basically have to negotiate this two part business, you know, one for the, for the recurring side and then one for the services side and they of course apply, you know, one multiple to one part of the business and another multiple to the other part of the business.
Yeah, it is pretty straightforward to do that.
But yeah, you're right.
Yeah, it would drag your valuation down if you let it too much.
Okay.
And then profitable.
Are you, are you profitable?
Do you have debt?
Yeah, profitable.
We've got a ton of debt.
We've bootstrapped the entire company and debt's been our, been our best friend.
So, so definitely would say that, that you know, venture debt loans, SBA emergency, you know, economic injury disaster loans, but.
You had it all.
Yeah, yeah.
All told, we're probably 4 million across everything.
About a million of that's to me personally.
This is my, my fifth company that I've created, so definitely would say that debt has been the engine for us.
And of course the other interesting part is when you're billing annual subscriptions and you're collecting the money up front, your customers are a little bit of your source of future funds.
Right.
So as long as you're growing, you know, you're collecting in advance and you use the, the collections as money to you know, sort of power things.
Okay.
How was your exits on those other businesses?
You got, you got out.
Yeah, yeah.
Of the four that preceded this one, I had Two successful, one absolute disaster and one push.
The push was we was the first one actually.
We raised $31 million in 1999 and, and sold the company to Nielsen for $31 million.
So we kind of took the money and handed it across to the investors who weren't, who weren't at all happy with the fact that they gave us $31 million for.
Yeah, they got their money back.
But, but, but remember in between 1999 and 2004, there was a lot that happened in there.
You know, you got the dot com bubble just bust and you say, yeah.
So we sort of thought we were hero.
Didn't.
Okay.
And so no investors.
You're 100%?
Oh, no.
Yeah, we do have investors.
So we acquired a company in 2013 for, you know, stock and taking over their debt and they had been funded.
They, they'd had $6 million in venture capital investment from LAR or Hippo Ventures is the biggest investor.
So they're, you know, now technically our biggest investor.
They're at about 11, 12%.
You know, a few others, some big names, you know, definitely like having them on the, you know, on the advisory board.
But, but yeah, they didn't invest in us directly.
They invested in what they thought would be the next Instagram.
And when it turned out, you know, that wasn't going to be the case, we were the booby prize.
Huh.
Okay.
And is those bits of IP that went into ypulse, are they still active or.
Yeah, it was worth merging and taking the down.
Yeah.

Basically what Thumb was was a, a social, a local social mobile app where 2 million kids went to ask and answer each other's questions and we absorbed that IP into, into how we, into how we do everything day to day.
So it was a good acquisition, but the app itself doesn't exist anymore.
If you also remember around 2012, 2013, we did the deal in June of 2013.
So there was a vibrant mobile app economy that since sort of had a bit of a, what would you call it, ass kicking.
Yeah, crushed by the social media networks.
Okay, fair enough.
So you kind of hedged your bets, but you've ended up even out the back of that.
But so 6 million in venture capital to return on the exit, which is I guess driving you as well to make sure you get that great valuation.
Yeah, a good price.
You've still got some, some change.
And, and in terms of the size of the team, how, how big is the team?
That's, yeah, 22 people, you know, pulling in 6 million.
So, you know, Revenue per headcount just a little under the 300,000 level, which, you know, is, is okay, it the biggest thing in terms of.
And our margins are about 66% right now, so decent margins.
What would make it better would be larger, more expensive sales force.
If I was to say the dream candidate, it would be somebody with a large and international sales force.
We've got a sales team of two people and they're based in North America.

And it shows of our 100 or so clients, there's less than 10 are outside of North America or outside of the US so definitely would say, I mean, we're collecting data in the U.S. canada, UK, France, Germany, Italy and Spain, but we're selling it to big US companies that are, you know, global in nature.
Yeah.
Okay.
And I've got like a, I got a three page kind of teaser that.
I. Yeah, please send it.
Yeah, that'd be great.
That'll kind of help frame it.
Definitely would say that that AI has been a big driver for us.
We jumped on that 18 months ago.
We held 15 billion data points under management, which is about a decade's worth of collecting surveys with young people.
And the power of AI to really unleash that is astounding.

So the kinds of companies that we talk to are media companies that want this sort of AI powered intelligence at the core of what they do, or agencies that want to sort of create an AI driven marketing kind of entity where that data at the core of it is, you know, is, is driving everything.
So I don't know if you, if you know about Publicis and the fact that they're like a very data driven agency.
And so, you know, data at the core of it really helps.
So we could definitely be like the crown jewel of a media company, you know, using that, the power of that data to kind of help their markets a little bit.
You know what Meta is doing, right.
Meta's trying to use AI to sort of make it so that, you know, marketers are just having a disproportionate impact based on the intelligence of what the tools are helping them with.
But I could demo that.
It's great stuff.

Definitely would say that if your client has an interest in large Fortune 500 companies and quite frankly doesn't, it's that kind of tool set that allows them to kind of really come in the door with, with a strategy that then they can execute upon.
Yeah, okay, great.
So you, so you do have like a sort of back end that you can demo to.
Oh yeah.
Okay, cool.
Yeah, I mean I wasn't, to be honest with you, I wasn't really expecting this to be the product.
So, yeah, I mean, it's great.
This is, this is the jewel in the crown, actually.
And a lot of our, funnily enough, a lot of our UK clients over the Americas.
Sorry, I think I froze for a second.
Yeah, you did.
You said a lot of your UK clients over your American clients.
Yeah.
Looking more for this sort of data thing to plug in.
I don't know, I'm sure it's, there are plenty of Americans out there as well that are looking for this.

But it's interesting, you know, I've been reading a lot on the sort of private equity and VC front, but like European companies, because you guys have been lowering rates faster and for longer, you're outpacing North America in terms of deal flow and M and A activity, you know, just because your, your monetary policy isn't quite as restrictive over there as over here.

So it would make sense that there would be a bunch of folks in the UK thinking, you know, now's the time for us to go shopping in America when, you know, their monetary policy is hurting, you know, their companies, whereas our monetary policy is enabling our M and A efforts.
Yeah, yeah, it possibly is that, but I think it's just that it's the data aspect in particular the more interesting.
Obviously there's a load of more, more sort of technical enabled businesses in the US anyway.
But also we, we've done a few deals in Israel as well where the tech, tech stuff in Israel is really good as well.
Yeah.
Dan, you've obviously got a great business.
My, my gut feeling is if we were to make an offer before next year, then it would be too low based on what your exit needs to be.
So I think I'm going to say to my client that we need to wait and speak to you in the middle of next year and try and get in before that process starts.
But right now it wouldn't be the right time for you to sell anyway and they're not going to overpay for something even though there's a lot more competition for these types of platforms.
So I think possibly it's a watch and see with you guys until next year, but you've got a fascinating business.
It looks absolutely brilliant.
Nothing like printing cash at the end of the month as well.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
When all those subscriptions come in.
So thank you for your time and I really do appreciate him being open.
But yeah, I think I'm going to stick something in my calendar for next.
Next June, I think, before everybody goes on holiday.
Yeah.
In touch and see where you guys are at and whether you'll.

Tell you what, maybe let's try for April instead, because I do feel like, you know, the wheels will be moving forward, you know, after we get our Q1 results and kind of see what the trajectory is between Q4 and Q1.
Okay.
And I will send.
I will send you that three page.
Yeah.
If you send that teaser over, that would be great.
Take a look at that.
All right.
Fantastic.
Enjoy the rest of your day, Dan.
Really appreciate it.
Thanks, Andrew.
Speak soon.

summary.overview:
- **Exit Target:** Formal exit process aimed for September 2026, targeting a $20 million valuation based on revenue multiples.  
- **Revenue Breakdown:** Current revenues at $5.85 million, 85% from subscriptions, 15% from services, underlining valuation importance.  
- **Market Position:** Operates as a subscription platform for over 100 Fortune 500 clients, collecting 400,000 interviews yearly in seven countries.  
- **Financial Health:** Profitable with 22 employees, revenue per employee just under $300,000, maintaining solid margins around 66%.  
- **Data Differentiation:** AI-powered platform manages 15 billion data points, enhancing insights and positioning as a valuable asset for large media firms.  
- **Sales Strategy:** Focus on Fortune 500 in North America; future investment needed in international sales team to increase market reach and revenue.
summary.short_summary: The company plans a formal exit process aimed for September 2026, targeting a $20 million valuation based on revenue multiples while avoiding tariff-related disruptions. Dan Coates highlighted the impact of tariffs on the footwear and retail sectors, which caused a slowdown in business but is rebounding. Current revenues are at $5.85 million, with 85% from subscriptions, and maintaining services below 15% of revenue is crucial for valuation. The company primarily operates as a subscription-based platform with over 100 Fortune 500 clients and limited competition. Financially, it is profitable with solid margins, despite carrying around $4 million in debt. The core product is an AI-powered youth marketing platform, and the sales strategy currently focuses on North American clients, with plans to expand internationally. The favorable M&A environment suggests waiting until mid-2024 to maximize valuation.
